claims.evidence: This is observed in TIRF imaging experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: When septin concentration was increased to values of 100 nM and higher, a fibrillar meshwork of septin filaments was suddenly observed.
claims.source: Remarkably, when we increased the septin concentration to values of 100 nM and higher, we suddenly observed a fibrillar meshwork of septin filaments.
claims.evidence: This is observed in TIRF imaging experiments.

claims.claim: At concentrations above 200 nM, septin bundles were present in the solution above the bilayer in addition to the membrane-bound septin meshwork.
claims.source: At concentrations above 200 nM, we found by off-TIRF-angle imaging that, in addition to the membrane-bound septin meshwork, also septin bundles were present in the solution above the bilayer, consistent with the observed onset for bundling in the absence of an adhesive membrane (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is observed by off-TIRF-angle imaging.

claims.claim: Membrane-bound septins exhibited negligible subunit exchange.
claims.source: Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching experiments showed that the membrane-bound septins exhibited negligible subunit exchange (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), indicating that they are stably anchored to the membrane.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments.

claims.claim: The membrane underneath the septin film was fluid, as indicated by FRAP measurements of rhodamine-labeled PE tracer lipids.
claims.source: The membrane underneath the septin film was nevertheless fluid, as indicated by FRAP measurements of rhodamine-labeled PE tracer lipids (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments on lipids.

claims.claim: Septin hexamers formed densely packed arrays of thin filaments on lipid monolayers containing PS, PI(4,5)P2, or both.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 3A–C, septin hexamers formed densely packed arrays of thin filaments in all three cases, which is qualitatively consistent with the dense meshworks observed by TIRF microscopy.
claims.evidence: This is observed in TEM images.

claims.claim: Close inspection of the EM micrographs revealed paired septin filaments with an average center-to-center spacing of 5.7 ± 0.8 nm on monolayers containing PS plus PI(4,5)P2.
claims.source: Close inspection of the EM micrographs revealed paired septin filaments (black arrows point out examples) with an average center-to-center spacing of 5.7 ± 0.8 nm on monolayers containing PS plus PIP(4,5)P2 (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is measured from TEM images.

claims.claim: The width of individual septin filaments was in the range of 3.5–4 nm (3.6 ± 0.53 nm averaged over all lipid conditions).
claims.source: The width of the individual filaments was in the range of 3.5–4 nm (3.6 ± 0.53 nm (N = 60) averaged over all lipid conditions; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), consistent with the expected 4 nm width of fly septin hexamers (Mavrakis et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is measured from TEM images and consistent with previous structural data.

claims.claim: On monolayers containing 20% PS plus 5% PI(4,5)P2, paired filaments were bridged at intervals of 24 nm by single or double hexamer rods.
claims.source: On monolayers containing 20% PS plus 5% PI(4,5)P2, we could observe clear examples of paired filaments that were bridged at intervals of 24 nm by single or double hexamer rods (Figure 3C), recognizable by their lengths clustering around either 24 nm or 48 nm (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), respectively.
claims.evidence: This is observed in TEM images.

claims.claim: Bridges between paired filaments were either perpendicular to the filaments they bridged or under an angle.
claims.source: These bridges were either perpendicular to the filaments they bridged (blue arrowheads) or under an angle (red arrowheads; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1C for quantification).
claims.evidence: This is observed in TEM images.

claims.claim: Mammalian septin hexamers form comparable arrays of tightly paired filaments connected by orthogonally or diagonally oriented single filaments on lipid monolayers.
claims.source: We observed comparable arrays of tightly paired filaments connected by orthogonally or diagonally oriented single filaments for mammalian septins on lipid monolayers of the same composition (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is observed in TEM images of mammalian septins.

claims.claim: Similar arrays of filaments were previously observed for budding yeast septins.
claims.source: Similar arrays of filaments were previously also observed for budding yeast septins (Garcia et al., 2011; Bertin et al., 2010), suggesting that this architectural feature is conserved within eukaryotes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on yeast septins.

claims.claim: For mammalian septin hexamers, the paired filaments are intersected with a distinct set of thinner continuous filaments, creating a network of interconnected and perpendicular filaments.
claims.source: Instead, for the mammalian septin hexamers, the paired filaments (white arrows in Figure 3—figure supplement 2) are intersected with a distinct set of thinner continuous filaments (red arrows), creating a network of interconnected and perpendicular filaments.
claims.evidence: This is observed in TEM images of mammalian septins.

claims.claim: CryoEM images confirm the presence of paired septin filaments on PI(4,5)P2-containing lipid membranes.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 4, the cryoEM images confirm the presence of paired septin filaments on PI(4,5)P2-containing lipid membranes (examples are traced out by double red lines in Figure 4A–B).
claims.evidence: This is observed in cryoEM images.

claims.claim: The average center-to-center distance between filaments forming a pair in cryoEM was 5.7 ± 0.8 nm.
claims.source: The average center-to-center distance between the filaments forming a pair was 5.7 ± 0.8 nm (N = 40, see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), in excellent agreement with the negative stain images of septin filaments on lipid monolayers.
claims.evidence: This is measured from cryoEM images.

claims.claim: Single filaments or hexamers were occasionally observed in cryoEM, including some that appeared to interconnect filaments at an orthogonal or oblique angle.
claims.source: In addition, we occasionally observed single filaments or hexamers (examples are traced out by single red lines in Figure 4B) including some that appeared to interconnect filaments at an orthogonal or oblique angle (blue lines in Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is observed in cryoEM images.

claims.claim: The diameter of control vesicles was measured to be 358 ± 180 nm while the diameter of vesicles displaying septins was 542 ± 199 nm.
claims.source: An indication for curvature-dependent binding in our data is that the diameter of control vesicles was measured to be 358 ± 180 nm (N = 40) while the diameter of similar vesicles displaying septins was 542 ± 199 nm (N = 24), thus slightly higher, on average (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is measured from cryoEM images.

claims.claim: Vesicles decorated with septin filaments typically appeared to have a faceted contour, whereas vesicles alone usually retained their spherical shape in cryoEM.
claims.source: Vesicles decorated with septin filaments typically appeared to have a faceted contour, whereas vesicles alone usually retained their spherical shape in cryoEM.
claims.evidence: This is observed in cryoEM images.

claims.claim: Cryo-electron tomography gave clear evidence that septin filaments are membrane-bound.
claims.source: Cryo-electron tomography gave further clear evidence that septin filaments are indeed membrane-bound (see Figure 4C–D and Figure 4—video 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by cryo-tomography.

claims.claim: At 12 nM, septin hexamers formed threads of typically several micrometers in length that were sparsely and randomly distributed on the bilayer surface.
claims.source: At 12 nM, septin hexamers formed threads of typically several micrometers in length that were sparsely and randomly distributed on the bilayer surface (Figure 5A–B, left column).
claims.evidence: This is observed in AFM images.

claims.claim: At 12 nM, the apparent height of septin threads was mostly uniform at 5.1 ± 0.9 nm with a few notable exceptions around 12 nm.
claims.source: Their apparent height was mostly uniform at 5.1 ± 0.9 nm (N = 29), with a few notable exceptions around 12 nm (N = 2).
claims.evidence: This is measured from AFM images.

claims.claim: At 12 nM, most isolated threads had a width of 11.5 ± 1.6 nm while merged threads were wider (16.6 ± 0.9 nm).
claims.source: The apparent width showed two relatively broad but distinct populations: most isolated threads had a width of 11.5 ± 1.6 nm (N = 19), whereas all merged threads and a few isolated ones were wider (16.6 ± 0.9 nm; N = 12) (Figure 5C, left column, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is measured from AFM images.

claims.claim: At 24 nM, septin hexamers formed threads that were isolated in some places and concentrated in areas of enhanced density in other places.
claims.source: At 24 nM, septin hexamers formed threads that were isolated in some places and concentrated in areas of enhanced density in other places (Figure 5A–B, center column).
claims.evidence: This is observed in AFM images.

claims.claim: At 60 nM, the septin hexamers formed threads that densely covered the bilayer surface in closely apposed patches of aligned filaments, resembling nematic domains.
claims.source: At 60 nM, the septin hexamers formed threads that densely covered the bilayer surface (Figure 5A–B, right column) in closely apposed patches of aligned filaments, resembling nematic domains observed for other 2D arrays of densely packed semiflexible biopolymers (Zhang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is observed in AFM images.

claims.claim: At 60 nM, the smallest thread heights and widths observed were comparable to those observed at 12 nM, indicating isolated single or paired filaments were still present.
claims.source: The smallest thread heights and widths observed were comparable to those observed at 12 nM, indicating isolated single or paired filaments were still present.
claims.evidence: This is measured from AFM images.

claims.claim: At 60 nM, some threads appeared much wider (up to a few 100 nm) suggesting that many single filaments may closely align on the lipid membrane.
claims.source: Other threads appeared much wider (up to a few 100 nm; Figure 5C, right column). This suggests that many (up to several tens of) single filaments may closely align on the lipid membrane, although the lateral resolution was insufficient to reveal the individual filaments and their spacing.
claims.evidence: This is measured from AFM images.

claims.claim: At 60 nM, wider threads had an elevated height, mostly between 8 and 13 nm and occasionally up to 18 nm, suggesting that septins also stacked on top of each other.
claims.source: The wider threads also had an elevated height, mostly between 8 and 13 nm and occasionally up to 18 nm (Figure 5C, right column), suggesting that septins also stacked on top of each other.
claims.evidence: This is measured from AFM images.

claims.claim: The morphologies of unfixed septins resembled those of GTA-fixed ones, though imaging unfixed septins was challenging because the filaments were more easily disrupted by the AFM tip.
claims.source: Importantly, the morphologies of unfixed septins resembled those of GTA-fixed ones, though imaging in this case was challenging because the filaments were more easily disrupted by the AFM tip (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is observed by comparing AFM images of fixed and unfixed samples.

claims.claim: Isolated filaments had heights of 4 nm, corresponding to the height of a single septin hexamer and thus a single layer of septin filaments.
claims.source: Here, we observed that the isolated filaments had heights of 4 nm, corresponding to the height of a single septin hexamer and thus a single layer of septin filaments, while the bundled areas had heights between 8 nm and 12 nm, suggesting that septin filaments can stack on top of each other.
claims.evidence: This is measured from AFM images.

claims.claim: Bundled areas had heights between 8 nm and 12 nm, suggesting that septin filaments can stack on top of each other.
claims.source: while the bundled areas had heights between 8 nm and 12 nm, suggesting that septin filaments can stack on top of each other.
claims.evidence: This is measured from AFM images.

claims.claim: In sparsely covered bilayer regions, wider bundles generally remained stable whereas narrower bundles or isolated filaments sometimes appeared ragged, suggesting that the AFM tip moved them along the membrane.
claims.source: In sparsely covered bilayer regions, wider bundles generally remained stable whereas narrower bundles or isolated filaments (both GTA-fixed and unfixed) sometimes appeared ragged, suggesting that the AFM tip moved them along the membrane (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B).
claims.evidence: This is observed in consecutive AFM scans.

claims.claim: Densely covered regions formed at 60 nM septins were completely unchanged after three consecutive 10 min scans, both for GTA-fixed and unfixed samples.
claims.source: Densely covered regions formed at 60 nM septins were completely unchanged after three consecutive 10 min scans, again both for GTA-fixed and unfixed samples (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C,D).
claims.evidence: This is observed in consecutive AFM scans.

claims.claim: Lateral associations among septin filaments within bundles or dense arrays may cause mechanical stabilization.
claims.source: These observations suggest that lateral associations among septin filaments within bundles or dense arrays may cause mechanical stabilization.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that dense arrays are more stable than isolated filaments.

claims.claim: Entire bundles can be laterally displaced along the membrane owing to lateral forces exerted by the AFM tip, resulting in permanent local kinks.
claims.source: Some image sequences clearly showed that entire bundles can be laterally displaced along the membrane owing to lateral forces exerted by the AFM tip. Interestingly, these events did not destroy the bundles but resulted in permanent local kinks, suggesting the septin filaments are intrinsically stiff and ductile but the link to the membrane is fluid.
claims.evidence: This is observed in consecutive AFM scans shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Septin filaments are intrinsically stiff and ductile but the link to the membrane is fluid.
claims.source: Interestingly, these events did not destroy the bundles but resulted in permanent local kinks, suggesting the septin filaments are intrinsically stiff and ductile but the link to the membrane is fluid.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation of bundle displacement without destruction.

claims.claim: The maximum thickness of the septin films at 60 nM was approximately 18 nm according to AFM height profiles.
claims.source: The maximum thickness of the septin films at 60 nM was approximately 18 nm, according to the height profiles.
claims.evidence: This is measured from AFM images.

claims.claim: SUV perfusion on a plain silica surface caused immediate changes in Δf and ΔD in a two-stage process characteristic for the initial adsorption of intact SUVs followed by SUV rupture, spreading and coalescence.
claims.source: SUV perfusion on a plain silica surface (Figure 7A) caused immediate changes in Δf and ΔD in a two-stage process that is characteristic for the initial adsorption of intact SUVs to the sensor surface followed by SUV rupture, spreading and coalescence (Richter et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is observed in QCM-D measurements and consistent with known SLB formation mechanisms.

claims.claim: The final shifts of Δf = −25 ± 1 Hz and ΔD < 0.2 × 10−6 are typical for confluent SLBs composed of PC and PS of high quality.
claims.source: The final shifts of Δf = −25 ± 1 Hz and ΔD < 0.2 × 10−6 (N = 6) are typical for confluent SLBs composed of PC and PS of high quality, that is, with a negligible quantity of residual intact vesicles (Richter et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is measured by QCM-D and consistent with previous characterization of SLBs.

claims.claim: Septin hexamer perfusion at 60 nM on SLBs produced an immediate decrease of Δf and a concurrent increase of ΔD, indicating that septins adsorbed.
claims.source: Septin hexamer perfusion at 60 nM on such a SLB (Figure 7B) produced an immediate decrease of Δf and a concurrent increase of ΔD, indicating that septins adsorbed.
claims.evidence: This is observed in QCM-D measurements.

claims.claim: Septin binding reached a plateau after about 50 min, and subsequent perfusion with buffer caused no appreciable change in Δf, suggesting that septin hexamers stably adsorb to the membrane.
claims.source: Binding reached a plateau after about 50 min, and subsequent perfusion with buffer caused no appreciable change in Δf, suggesting that septin hexamers stably adsorb to the membrane.
claims.evidence: This is observed in QCM-D measurements.

claims.claim: The saturation of the QCM-D signal despite continued perfusion with septin hexamers indicates the presence of a mechanism that limits septin binding and film growth.
claims.source: Moreover, the saturation of the signal despite continued perfusion with septin hexamers indicates the presence of a mechanism that limits septin binding and film growth.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the QCM-D data showing signal saturation.

claims.claim: Similar binding kinetics and self-limiting levels of binding were observed on SLBs containing 5% PI(4,5)P2, or a combination of 5% PI(4,5)P2 and 20% PS.
claims.source: We observed similar binding kinetics and self-limiting levels of binding on SLBs containing 5% PI(4,5)P2, or a combination of 5% PI(4,5)P2 and 20% PS (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This is observed in QCM-D measurements.

claims.claim: No adhesion of septin hexamers to pure PC membranes was observed.
claims.source: In contrast, we did not observe any adhesion of septin hexamers to pure PC membranes (Figure 7B; dotted blue line with diamonds).
claims.evidence: This is observed in QCM-D measurements.

claims.claim: The presence of negatively charged lipids is required for septin-membrane binding.
claims.source: We conclude that the presence of negatively charged lipids is required for septin-membrane binding, consistent with the TIRF observations, and that film growth is self-limiting.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from QCM-D and TIRF experiments.

claims.claim: The total frequency shift for septin binding was Δf = -93 ± 4 Hz on SLBs containing 20%PS.
claims.source: The total frequency shift for septin binding was Δf = -93 ± 4 Hz (N = 4) on SLBs containing 20%PS
claims.evidence: This is measured by QCM-D.

claims.claim: The total frequency shift for septin binding was Δf = -77 ± 2 Hz on SLBs containing 5% PI(4,5)P2.
claims.source: Δf = -77 ± 2 Hz (N = 2) on SLBs containing 5% PI(4,5)P2
claims.evidence: This is measured by QCM-D.

claims.claim: The total frequency shift for septin binding was Δf = -113 ± 7 Hz on SLBs containing both 5% PI(4,5)P2 and 20% PS.
claims.source: and Δf = -113 ± 7 Hz (N = 2) on SLBs containing both 5% PI(4,5)P2 and 20% PS (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is measured by QCM-D.

claims.claim: Using the Sauerbrey equation, septin film thickness values are estimated to be 15 nm on SLBs containing 20% PS, 13 nm on SLBs containing 5% PI(4,5)P2, and 19 nm on SLBs containing both 5% PI(4,5)P2 and 20% PS.
claims.source: Using the Sauerbrey equation (see Eq. (1) Nishihama et al., 2011), we estimate septin film thickness values of 15 nm on SLBs containing 20% PS, 13 nm on SLBs containing 5% PI(4,5)P2, and 19 nm on SLBs containing both 5% PI(4,5)P2 and 20% PS, from the respective frequency shifts.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from QCM-D frequency shifts using the Sauerbrey equation.

claims.claim: The estimated film thicknesses from QCM-D are consistent with the upper end of bundle heights measured by AFM.
claims.source: This is consistent with the upper end of bundle heights measured by AFM (Figure 5C, right column), which we had attributed to stacking into more than one layer.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison between QCM-D and AFM measurements.

claims.claim: Membrane-bound septins attained dissipation over frequency shift ratios ΔD/-Δf between (0.20 ± 0.01)×10−6/Hz at low coverage and (0.09 ± 0.01)×10−6/Hz at high coverage.
claims.source: Membrane-bound septins attained dissipation over frequency shift ratios ΔD/-Δf between (0.20 ± 0.01)×10−6/Hz at low coverage (Δf = −15 ± 5 Hz) and (0.09 ± 0.01)×10−6/Hz at high coverage (Δf < −90 Hz; N = 4; Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is measured from QCM-D data.

claims.claim: The higher ΔD/-Δf ratios for septins are consistent with a high degree of flexibility in the linkage between the coiled coils and the globular domains of septin hexamers.
claims.source: The higher ΔD/-Δf ratios for septins are consistent with a high degree of flexibility in the linkage between the coiled coils and the globular domains of septin hexamers.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of ΔD/-Δf ratios with other proteins.

claims.claim: C-terminally truncated fly septin hexamers (ΔCC mutant) form stable hexamers.
claims.source: Transmission EM confirmed that fly septins with their C-termini truncated from all subunits form stable hexamers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), similarly to C-terminally truncated human septin hexamers (Sirajuddin et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is observed in TEM images and consistent with previous studies on human septins.

claims.claim: In low salt polymerization buffer, the ΔCC mutant only formed short rods with lengths varying continuously between ~20 and ~80 nm.
claims.source: EM imaging showed that in low salt polymerization buffer, the ΔCC mutant only formed short rods (Figure 8A–B) with lengths varying continuously between ~20 and ~80 nm (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is observed in TEM images.

claims.claim: On lipid monolayers, the C-terminally truncated fly septin hexamers formed dense arrays of aligned filaments.
claims.source: However, on lipid monolayers the C-terminally truncated fly septin hexamers formed dense arrays of aligned filaments (Figure 8C–F).
claims.evidence: This is observed in TEM images.

claims.claim: Membrane-binding promotes filament formation for C-terminally truncated septins, mirroring earlier observations for yeast septin octamers with C-terminally truncated Cdc11 subunits.
claims.source: Thus, membrane-binding promotes filament formation, mirroring earlier observations for yeast septin octamers with C-terminally truncated Cdc11 subunits (Bertin et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison with yeast septin behavior.

claims.claim: The width of the ΔCC septin filaments was on average slightly smaller than that of full length septin filaments, around 3.5 nm.
claims.source: The width of the ΔCC septin filaments was on average slightly smaller than that of full length septin filaments, around 3.5 nm (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), likely due to the absence of coiled coils.
claims.evidence: This is measured from TEM images.

claims.claim: In some places, three ΔCC septin filaments can be seen side by side instead of two.
claims.source: In places we can see three filaments side by side instead of two (indicated by triple blue lines in Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: This is observed in TEM images.

claims.claim: The mutant ΔCC filaments were more closely spaced than wild type septin filaments, with a center-to-center distance for filaments within pairs of around 4.5 nm.
claims.source: The mutant filaments were even more closely spaced than wild type septin filaments, with a center-to-center distance for filaments within pairs of around 4.5 nm (Figure 8G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), consistent with direct contact between the globular domains deprived of the CC domain of adjacent filaments due to crowding and perhaps specific G-domain interactions.
claims.evidence: This is measured from TEM images.

claims.claim: The septin density on the lipid monolayers observed in EM images for the ΔCC mutant was notably higher than for the full-length septins, even though the solution concentrations were the same.
claims.source: The septin density on the lipid monolayers observed in EM images for the ΔCC mutant was notably higher than for the full-length septins, even though the solution concentrations were the same.
claims.evidence: This is observed by comparing TEM images of ΔCC and full-length septins.

claims.claim: The ΔCC mutant binds to bilayers but the frequency shift is much smaller than for the full-length septins, indicating a thinner layer.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 7C, the ΔCC mutant binds to the bilayers but the frequency shift is much smaller than for the full-length septins, indicating a thinner layer.
claims.evidence: This is measured by QCM-D.

claims.claim: For the ΔCC mutant, the -Δf values remained less than 10 Hz, consistent with a single septin monolayer.
claims.source: In this case, the -Δf values remained less than 10 Hz, consistent with a single septin monolayer.
claims.evidence: This is measured by QCM-D.

claims.claim: The coiled coils are not needed for membrane binding, but they are needed for filament pairing, the formation of cross-bridges, and the stacking of septins on top of each other.
claims.source: Thus, the EM and QCM-D data demonstrate that the coiled coils are not needed for membrane binding, but they are needed for filament pairing, the formation of cross-bridges, and the stacking of septins on top of each other.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the comparison of ΔCC and full-length septin behavior.

claims.claim: Fly septin hexamers have a high affinity for negatively charged lipid bilayers, which competes with the septin–septin lateral interactions that prevail in bulk solution.
claims.source: Fluorescence imaging revealed that fly septin hexamers have a high affinity for negatively charged lipid bilayers, which competes with the septin–septin lateral interactions that prevail in bulk solution, and that they form dense membrane-associated meshworks.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF imaging experiments.

claims.claim: Fly septin hexamers form dense membrane-associated meshworks.
claims.source: Fluorescence imaging revealed that fly septin hexamers have a high affinity for negatively charged lipid bilayers, which competes with the septin–septin lateral interactions that prevail in bulk solution, and that they form dense membrane-associated meshworks.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF imaging experiments.

claims.claim: Electron microscopy imaging revealed that septin meshworks are predominantly comprised of paired filaments and meshworks thereof.
claims.source: Electron microscopy (EM) imaging revealed that these meshworks are predominantly comprised of paired filaments and meshworks thereof.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by TEM and cryoEM imaging.

claims.claim: A similar organization of paired filaments was observed for mammalian septin hexamers.
claims.source: A similar organization was observed for mammalian septin hexamers, consistent with earlier findings for septin-containing porcine brain extracts (Tanaka-Takiguchi et al., 2009; Yamada et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by TEM imaging and consistent with previous studies.

claims.claim: Atomic force microscopy of septins on lipid bilayers showed that septin filaments laterally associate into bundles but also stack on top of each other.
claims.source: Finally, atomic force microscopy (AFM) of septins on lipid bilayers showed that septin filaments laterally associate into bundles but also stack on top of each other.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by AFM imaging.

claims.claim: AFM imaging, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching and QCM-D experiments indicate that the septins are immobile and firmly attached to the membrane.
claims.source: AFM imaging, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching and QCM-D experiments indicate that the septins are immobile and firmly attached to the membrane.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by multiple experimental techniques.

claims.claim: C-terminally truncated septin hexamers form monolayers and the filaments do not form pairs and meshworks, showing that the coiled coils of septins are crucial for mediating septin-septin interactions.
claims.source: By contrast, C-terminally truncated septin hexamers form monolayers and the filaments do not form pairs and meshworks, showing that the coiled coils of septins are crucial for mediating septin-septin interactions.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with ΔCC mutants.

claims.claim: Membrane binding catalyzes animal septin polymerization.
claims.source: Our findings establish that membrane binding catalyzes animal septin polymerization and has a dramatic impact on septin self-assembly, with C-terminal coiled-coils playing a key role in higher order septin filament organization.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the comparison of septin assembly in solution vs on membranes.

claims.claim: Membrane binding has a dramatic impact on septin self-assembly.
claims.source: Our findings establish that membrane binding catalyzes animal septin polymerization and has a dramatic impact on septin self-assembly, with C-terminal coiled-coils playing a key role in higher order septin filament organization.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: C-terminal coiled-coils play a key role in higher order septin filament organization.
claims.source: Our findings establish that membrane binding catalyzes animal septin polymerization and has a dramatic impact on septin self-assembly, with C-terminal coiled-coils playing a key role in higher order septin filament organization.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the comparison of full-length and ΔCC mutant septins.

claims.claim: For fly septin hexamers, the threshold for polymerization is lowered more than 10-fold, from 200 nM in solution to less than 12 nM on negatively charged membranes.
claims.source: For fly septin hexamers, the threshold for polymerization is lowered more than 10-fold, from 200 nM in solution to less than 12 nM on negatively charged membranes (Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing TIRF and AFM data for septins in solution vs on membranes.

claims.claim: The polymerization-enhancing effect of membrane binding is likely due to the increase of the effective septin concentration caused by 2D confinement.
claims.source: The polymerization-enhancing effect of membrane binding is likely due to the increase of the effective septin concentration caused by 2D confinement.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on general principles of 2D confinement.

claims.claim: Membrane binding may orient septins in a manner that promotes their polymerization, as seen for other proteins such as annexin A5.
claims.source: In addition, membrane binding may orient septins in a manner that promotes their polymerization, as seen for other proteins such as annexin A5 (Oling et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by analogy to other proteins.

claims.claim: Both animal and yeast septins form paired filaments visible by transmission electron microscopy, with a narrow spacing of ~2 nm.
claims.source: A second similarity between the behavior of animal and yeast septins on membranes is that they both form paired filaments visible by transmission electron microscopy, with a narrow spacing of ~2 nm, much narrower than the ~10 nm spacing observed for yeast septin filaments formed in solution (Bertin et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is observed in TEM images and compared to previous studies on yeast septins.

claims.claim: Paired filaments of both animal and yeast septins are interconnected by bridges visible by electron microscopy, which appear to be formed by short and thin (single) septin filaments having a length and axial spacing that correspond to the length of a single protomer.
claims.source: A third similarity is that paired filaments of both animal and yeast septins are interconnected by bridges visible by electron microscopy, which appear to be formed by short and thin (single) septin filaments having a length and axial spacing that correspond to the length of a single protomer (Bertin et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is observed in TEM images and compared to previous studies on yeast septins.

claims.claim: Similar arrays of septin filaments have been observed by electron microscopy in yeast cells.
claims.source: Similar arrays have been observed by electron microscopy in yeast cells (Ong et al., 2014), but not yet in animal cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Fly septins form thick and rigid bundles with tapered ends in solution, suggesting that the septins have strong lateral interactions that promote bundling.
claims.source: Fly septins form thick and rigid bundles with tapered ends in solution, suggesting that the septins have strong lateral interactions that promote bundling.
claims.evidence: This is observed in TIRF and STEM imaging.

claims.claim: On membranes, there is a gradual transition from dilute arrays of thick bundles to dense arrays of paired filaments with increasing net surface charge, suggesting a competition of septin-membrane interactions with lateral septin-septin interactions.
claims.source: On membranes, however, we observed by TIRF microscopy a gradual transition from dilute arrays of thick bundles to dense arrays of paired filaments with increasing net surface charge. This observation suggests a competition of septin-membrane interactions with lateral septin-septin interactions, which suppresses the formation of thick bundles on membranes.
claims.evidence: This is observed in TIRF imaging experiments.

claims.claim: Yeast septin octamers tend to form paired filaments in solution.
claims.source: By contrast, yeast septin octamers tend to form paired filaments in solution (Bertin et al., 2008; Bertin et al., 2010) (as confirmed by quantitative mass-mapping STEM in our study, see Figure 1E), although they do form bundles under certain conditions (Booth and Thorner, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and confirmed by STEM in this study.

claims.claim: In solution fly septins have a stronger propensity for bundling than yeast septins, but on membranes the two septins behave similarly.
claims.source: Thus, in solution fly septins have a stronger propensity for bundling than yeast septins, but on membranes the two septins behave similarly.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the comparison of fly and yeast septin behavior.

claims.claim: Fly septins form similar structures on membranes containing PS or PI(4,5)P2, and the main determinant of fly septin binding and filament organization in both cases is the net surface charge of the membrane.
claims.source: We find that fly septins form similar structures on membranes containing PS or PI(4,5)P2, and that the main determinant of fly septin binding and filament organization in both cases is the net surface charge of the membrane.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from TIRF and EM experiments with different lipid compositions.

claims.claim: Cdc11-capped yeast septin octamers are highly selective for PI, PI(4)P, PI(5)P and PI(4,5)P2, while they do not interact with PS.
claims.source: By contrast, Cdc11-capped yeast septin octamers were shown to be highly selective for PI, PI(4)P, PI(5)P and PI(4,5)P2, while they did not interact with PS (Khan et al., 2018; Bridges et al., 2016; Bertin et al., 2010; Beber, 2018; Cannon et al., 2019; Bridges et al., 2014; Casamayor and Snyder, 2003; Onishi et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on yeast septins.

claims.claim: Septins interact with negatively charged phospholipids via a polybasic region close to the N-terminus that is composed of a sequence of 1–7 basic amino acids.
claims.source: It is thought that septins interact with negatively charged phospholipids via a polybasic region close to the N-terminus that is composed of a sequence of 1–7 basic amino acids (Zhang et al., 1999; Casamayor and Snyder, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The polybasic stretch in septins is very similar to polybasic sequences found in gelsolin, profilin, G-protein-coupled receptor kinases and ion channels, which are all reported to interact with PI(4,5)P2.
claims.source: This stretch is very similar to polybasic sequences found in gelsolin, profilin, G-protein-coupled receptor kinases and ion channels (Zhang et al., 1999), which are all reported to interact with PI(4,5)P2.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The intricate, highly organized septin filament meshworks observed at the membrane of dividing budding yeast have not been documented to date in animal cells.
claims.source: It is noteworthy that the intricate, highly organized septin filament meshworks observed at the membrane of dividing budding yeast (Bertin et al., 2012; Ong et al., 2014) have not been documented to date in animal cells.
claims.evidence: This is based on a review of the literature.

claims.claim: Cdc11 and Shs1 have C-termini that are 2–3 times longer than their animal counterparts.
claims.source: Cdc11/Shs1 have C-termini that are 2–3 times longer than their animal counterparts (118 and 211 residues for Cdc11 and Shs1 vs 55 and 57 residues for SEPT2 and DSep1, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claims.claim: Cdc11 and Shs1 termini are predicted to form coiled-coils twice as long as the ones of SEPT2/DSep1.
claims.source: Cdc11 and Shs1 termini are predicted to form coiled-coils twice as long as the ones of SEPT2/DSep1, and with flexible hinges between the α6 helix and the coiled-coils 2–3 times longer than their animal counterparts (Figure 1B,C and Taveneau et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is based on coiled-coil prediction analysis.

claims.claim: The very high conservation between fly and mammalian septins (on the order of 65–75% identity) suggests that studying animal septin assembly promises to advance our understanding of how differences between yeast and animal septins lead to differences in their organization and function.
claims.source: Given the above differences between yeast and animal septins, the very high conservation between fly and mammalian septins (on the order of 65–75% identity), and the ubiquitous presence and essential functions of animal septins, studying animal septin assembly promises to advance our understanding of how differences between yeast and animal septins lead to differences in their organization and function.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the research based on sequence conservation.

results.result: Fly septin hexamers are highly homologous to human septins (65-75% identity) and have a predicted palindromic arrangement with Pnut in the center, DSep1 at the termini, and DSep2 in between.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C35 provide sequence identity data from alignment analysis, and C36 infers the palindromic arrangement from phylogenetic analysis and previous mammalian septin studies. The sequence homology is directly measured, and the structural arrangement is reasonably inferred from established phylogenetic relationships and recent structural data on mammalian septins.

results.result: Computational prediction indicates that fly septin C-termini form coiled-coils: DSep1 has a 28-residue (4 nm) coiled-coil, while DSep2 and Pnut have 86-residue (13 nm) coiled-coils.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C38 report predictions from the COILS algorithm, and C39-C40 calculate physical lengths based on standard alpha-helix parameters (1.5 Å/residue). The computational predictions are appropriately applied and the length calculations are mathematically correct. However, these remain predictions rather than experimentally determined structures.

results.result: In solution, fly septin hexamers form bundles at concentrations ≥200 nM, with rapid assembly (<2 min) producing stiff, straight bundles.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C45 are directly observed by TIRF microscopy (C42-C44 with data support) and inferred from bundle morphology (C45). The concentration threshold, kinetics, and mechanical properties are consistently documented across the imaging data. The inference of stiffness from lack of thermal undulations is reasonable.

results.result: Yeast septins form thin semiflexible paired filaments with mass-per-length of ~20 kDa/nm and occasional double-stranded structures with 17-27 nm spacing.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 are measured by STEM with TMV rods as mass standards. The MPL measurement (~20 kDa/nm) is close to the theoretical value for paired filaments (23.2 kDa/nm), and the double-stranded spacing is consistent with previous EM studies. The use of internal calibration standards strengthens the quantitative measurements.

results.result: Fly septin bundles in solution are 3D structures with concentration-dependent dimensions: at 200 nM, bundles have tapered ends with ~250 kDa/nm MPL and 31 nm width (≥3 monolayers); at 500 nM, bundles reach 280 nm width and ~5000 kDa/nm MPL (≥6 monolayers).
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 provide STEM measurements with quantitative analysis, while C53 infers 3D growth from the dimensional data. The MPL and width measurements are internally consistent, and the calculations of hexamer numbers per cross-section are mathematically sound. The inference of 3D rather than 2D growth is well-supported by the geometric analysis.

results.result: Fly septin hexamers bind to anionic lipid bilayers (PS and PI(4,5)P2) through electrostatic interactions, with membrane recruitment occurring rapidly (<3 min) and showing a transition from sparse bundles to dense layers with increasing anionic lipid content.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C59 are directly observed by TIRF imaging, C60 infers the electrostatic mechanism from the similar behavior on PS vs PI(4,5)P2, and C61 provides quantitative support by comparing the lipid concentrations needed for the transition. The inference of electrostatic interactions is well-supported by the comparative data showing that net charge, rather than specific lipid identity, governs binding. The rapid kinetics and concentration-dependent morphology are consistently documented.

results.result: On PS-containing bilayers, fly septins show concentration-dependent assembly: at 10-50 nM, only puncta are observed; at ≥100 nM, fibrillar meshworks form; above 200 nM, solution-phase bundles coexist with membrane-bound meshworks.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64 are observed by TIRF and off-TIRF-angle imaging. The concentration thresholds are clearly defined and the morphological transitions are well-documented. The observation that solution-phase bundling occurs above 200 nM is consistent with the earlier findings in C42-C43.

results.result: Membrane-bound septins are immobile with negligible subunit exchange, while the underlying lipid bilayer remains fluid.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 are demonstrated by FRAP experiments on both septins and lipids. The contrasting behavior (immobile septins vs. fluid lipids with D ≈ 1.2 μm²/s) is clearly documented and indicates stable septin-membrane attachment without compromising membrane fluidity.

results.result: On lipid monolayers containing PS and/or PI(4,5)P2, fly septin hexamers form densely packed arrays of paired filaments (5.7 ± 0.8 nm center-to-center spacing, 3.6 ± 0.53 nm width) with orthogonal or diagonal bridges at 24 nm intervals.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C71 are directly measured from TEM images. The filament dimensions are consistent with the expected 4 nm width of hexamers, and the bridge lengths correspond to single or double hexamer rods. The quantitative measurements are well-documented with appropriate sample sizes and error estimates.

results.result: Mammalian septin hexamers form similar paired filament arrays with orthogonal/diagonal connections on lipid monolayers, though with some structural differences from fly septins; similar arrays were previously observed for yeast septins.
results.evaluation: Claims C72 and C74 are observed in TEM images of mammalian septins, while C73 is supported by citations to previous yeast septin studies. The observation of conserved architectural features across species is well-documented, though the subtle differences (continuous vs. isolated bridging filaments) are noted.

results.result: CryoEM confirms paired septin filaments on PI(4,5)P2-containing vesicles with 5.7 ± 0.8 nm spacing, along with occasional single filaments and orthogonal/oblique interconnections.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 are observed in cryoEM images. The center-to-center spacing measurement is in excellent agreement with the negative stain EM data (C68), providing independent validation. The observation of single filaments and bridges is consistent with the monolayer data.

results.result: Septin-decorated vesicles are larger (542 ± 199 nm) than control vesicles (358 ± 180 nm) and show faceted contours, with cryo-tomography confirming membrane binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 are measured from cryoEM images, and C80 is demonstrated by cryo-tomography. The size difference suggests curvature-dependent binding, and the faceting indicates membrane deformation by septins. The tomography provides definitive evidence of membrane association.

results.result: AFM reveals concentration-dependent septin organization on bilayers: at 12 nM, sparse threads (5.1 ± 0.9 nm height, 11.5-16.6 nm width); at 24 nM, mixed isolated and dense regions; at 60 nM, dense coverage with threads up to 100s of nm wide and 8-18 nm tall, suggesting lateral alignment and vertical stacking.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C88 are measured by AFM with appropriate quantification. The height and width distributions are consistent with single/paired filaments at low concentration and multilayer structures at high concentration. The inference of lateral alignment and vertical stacking from the dimensional data is reasonable, though tip convolution effects are acknowledged.

results.result: Unfixed septins show similar morphology to GTA-fixed samples, with isolated filaments at 4 nm height (single layer) and bundled areas at 8-12 nm height (stacked layers).
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C91 compare fixed and unfixed samples by AFM. The similar morphologies validate that fixation does not significantly alter structure. The height measurements directly support the interpretation of single vs. stacked layers, with 4 nm corresponding to the hexamer G-domain height.

results.result: AFM scanning reveals that dense septin arrays are mechanically stable while isolated filaments are more easily disrupted; bundles can be displaced without destruction, suggesting stiff, ductile filaments with fluid membrane attachment.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93 are observed in consecutive AFM scans, C94 infers mechanical stabilization from density-dependent stability, and C95-C96 infer mechanical properties from bundle displacement behavior. The observations are consistent across fixed and unfixed samples, and the inferences about mechanical properties are reasonable based on the displacement patterns.

results.result: QCM-D measurements show that septin hexamers stably bind to anionic lipid bilayers (PS and/or PI(4,5)P2) but not to neutral PC bilayers, with self-limiting film growth reaching maximum thickness of ~18 nm (by AFM) after ~50 min.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C105 combine AFM and QCM-D data. The QCM-D kinetics show stable binding with saturation, the lack of binding to PC confirms the requirement for anionic lipids, and the self-limiting growth is consistently observed across lipid compositions. The maximum thickness from AFM (C97) is consistent with the QCM-D estimates (C109-C110).

results.result: QCM-D frequency shifts indicate septin film thicknesses of 15 nm (20% PS), 13 nm (5% PI(4,5)P2), and 19 nm (20% PS + 5% PI(4,5)P2), consistent with AFM measurements.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108 report measured frequency shifts, C109 calculates thicknesses using the Sauerbrey equation, and C110 compares with AFM data. The calculations are appropriate for the Sauerbrey equation (assuming rigid films), and the consistency between QCM-D and AFM validates both measurements. However, the Sauerbrey equation assumes a rigid, uniform film, which may not fully apply given the ΔD values.

results.result: Membrane-bound septins show ΔD/-Δf ratios of 0.20 × 10⁻⁶/Hz (low coverage) to 0.09 × 10⁻⁶/Hz (high coverage), consistent with flexible linkages between coiled-coils and globular domains.
results.evaluation: Claim C111 reports measured ΔD/-Δf ratios, and C112 infers flexibility from comparison with other proteins. The ratios are higher than for rigid globular proteins, supporting the interpretation of flexible hinges. The comparison with other protein systems provides appropriate context.

results.result: C-terminally truncated (ΔCC) fly septin hexamers form stable hexamers that only form short rods (20-80 nm) in solution but assemble into dense arrays of aligned filaments on lipid monolayers, with filaments more closely spaced (4.5 nm) and slightly narrower (3.5 nm) than wild-type.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C120 are observed by TEM. The ΔCC mutant behavior demonstrates that membrane binding promotes polymerization even without coiled-coils, and the closer spacing suggests direct G-domain contacts. The comparison with yeast septin behavior (C116) provides appropriate context.

results.result: QCM-D shows that ΔCC septins bind to bilayers but form much thinner layers (-Δf < 10 Hz, consistent with monolayers), demonstrating that coiled-coils are not required for membrane binding but are essential for filament pairing, cross-bridging, and stacking.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C122 are measured by QCM-D, and C123 synthesizes the EM and QCM-D data to conclude the role of coiled-coils. The conclusion is well-supported by the contrasting behavior of wild-type (multilayer) vs. ΔCC (monolayer) septins. This is a key mechanistic finding.

results.result: Fly septin hexamers have high affinity for negatively charged bilayers and form dense, immobile membrane-associated meshworks of paired filaments that laterally associate and stack, with coiled-coils crucial for higher-order organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C130 synthesize findings from multiple techniques (TIRF, EM, AFM, FRAP, QCM-D). The high affinity, dense meshwork formation, paired filament structure, lateral association, stacking, and role of coiled-coils are all consistently documented across the different experimental approaches. This represents a comprehensive characterization.

results.result: Membrane binding catalyzes animal septin polymerization and has a dramatic impact on septin self-assembly, with C-terminal coiled-coils playing a key role in higher-order filament organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C133 are overarching conclusions synthesizing the entire study. The catalytic effect of membrane binding is demonstrated by the >10-fold reduction in polymerization threshold (C134), the dramatic impact is shown by the transition from 3D bundles to 2D arrays, and the role of coiled-coils is established by the ΔCC mutant experiments. These conclusions are well-supported by the comprehensive data.

results.result: Membrane binding lowers the polymerization threshold >10-fold (from 200 nM to <12 nM), likely due to 2D confinement increasing effective concentration and possibly orienting septins to promote polymerization.
results.evaluation: Claim C134 compares TIRF and AFM data for solution vs. membrane conditions, C135 proposes a mechanism based on 2D confinement, and C136 suggests an additional orientation mechanism by analogy to annexin A5. The quantitative comparison is well-documented, and the proposed mechanisms are reasonable, though C136 is more speculative.

results.result: Both animal and yeast septins form paired filaments (~2 nm spacing) on membranes that are interconnected by bridges corresponding to single protomers, with similar arrays observed in yeast cells but not yet in animal cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C138 compare the current findings with previous yeast septin studies, and C139 notes the lack of similar observations in animal cells. The comparisons are appropriately cited and highlight conserved features across species. The caveat about animal cells is important for contextualizing the in vitro findings.

results.result: Fly septins have stronger bundling propensity than yeast septins in solution, but on membranes both form similar paired filament structures, suggesting competition between septin-membrane and septin-septin interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C143 compare fly and yeast septin behavior in solution vs. on membranes. The stronger bundling of fly septins in solution is documented by TIRF and STEM (C140), the transition on membranes is observed by TIRF (C141), yeast behavior is confirmed by STEM and citations (C142), and the conclusion (C143) is well-supported by the comparative data.

results.result: Fly septins bind membranes based on net surface charge rather than specific lipid identity, contrasting with yeast septins that are highly selective for phosphoinositides; septins likely interact via N-terminal polybasic regions similar to other PI(4,5)P2-binding proteins.
results.evaluation: Claim C144 is concluded from the similar behavior on PS vs. PI(4,5)P2 membranes, C145 contrasts with yeast septin selectivity (cited), and C146-C147 discuss the likely binding mechanism (cited). The conclusion about electrostatic vs. specific binding is well-supported by the comparative lipid data, and the proposed mechanism is consistent with known polybasic-lipid interactions.

results.result: Yeast and animal septins differ in C-terminal length and coiled-coil structure (yeast 2-3× longer), which may explain differences in organization; the high conservation between fly and mammalian septins (65-75% identity) makes fly septins a valuable model for understanding animal septin function.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C150 compare structural features between yeast and animal septins based on sequence analysis and coiled-coil predictions, and C151 discusses the significance of studying fly septins. The structural comparisons are well-documented, and the rationale for using fly septins as a model is sound given the high conservation with mammalian septins.

results.result: Binding to flat lipid membranes requires electrostatic interactions with anionic lipids and promotes ordered self-assembly of fly septins into filamentous meshworks.
results.evaluation: These claims from the abstract are supported by the comprehensive experimental data showing: (1) no binding to neutral PC membranes (C104), (2) binding to PS and PI(4,5)P2 membranes with similar behavior suggesting electrostatic interactions (C60, C144), and (3) formation of ordered paired filament meshworks on membranes (C67-C71, C75-C77). The abstract claims accurately summarize the main findings.

results.result: Both fly and mammalian septins form arrays of single and paired filaments; fly filaments form mechanically rigid 12-18 nm thick double layers, while C-terminally truncated mutants form 4 nm monolayers, indicating coiled-coils are required for stacking.
results.evaluation: These abstract claims are supported by: TEM showing paired filaments for both fly and mammalian septins (C67, C72), AFM and QCM-D showing 12-18 nm thickness for wild-type (C88, C97, C109), and QCM-D showing 4 nm monolayers for ΔCC mutants (C122). The conclusion about coiled-coil requirement is well-supported by the ΔCC mutant data (C123).
